plan.contextChunk: This figure shows three rendered orbital shapes in a row on a white background, each captioned in bold beneath it, reading from left to right "An s orbital", "A p orbital", and "A d orbital". The leftmost is one translucent pink sphere, smooth and unbroken in every direction, with a small yellow-green bead at its center marking the nucleus. The middle shape stacks two lobes vertically, a rounded pink one above and a matching blue one below, meeting at a green nucleus bead; both are drawn as full, doorknob-like volumes rather than pointed teardrops, and they pinch away to nothing where they meet. The rightmost carries four lobes in a cloverleaf around a central green bead, their colors alternating around the ring: pink at the upper left and lower right, blue at the upper right and lower left. Color does the encoding, pink and blue standing for opposite algebraic signs of the wave function across a node, so the alternation shows the sign flipping with each crossing from one lobe to the next. The three together set out the orbital shapes and sign patterns that later account for bonding.

elements: s orbital: single smooth translucent pink sphere centered at origin
p orbital: upper rounded pink lobe (ellipsoid) above the nucleus
p orbital: lower rounded blue lobe (ellipsoid) below the nucleus, pinching to nothing at the origin
p orbital: horizontal nodal plane through the nucleus (faint translucent disk)
d orbital: four cloverleaf lobes in the XY plane at the 45-degree diagonals
d orbital: pink lobe upper-left and pink lobe lower-right
d orbital: blue lobe upper-right and blue lobe lower-left
d orbital: two nodal planes (the XZ and YZ planes) through the nucleus (faint translucent disks)
green nucleus bead at the center of each orbital
bold caption beneath the active orbital: 'An s orbital' / 'A p orbital' / 'A d orbital'
sign legend: pink = positive wave-function sign, blue = negative sign

interactions.label: Orbital
interactions.teaches: Switching s -> p -> d shows the lobe count growing (1 sphere, 2 lobes, 4 lobes) and the number of nodal planes growing (0, 1, 2), while the pink/blue sign coloring and the central nucleus stay consistent across all three

Clicking any pink lobe lights up every pink lobe and dims the blue ones (and vice versa), making clear that the two colors are not different materials but the opposite algebraic signs of the wave function on either side of a node

Rotating the volume reveals that each color boundary is a flat nodal plane passing through the nucleus: the p orbital has one horizontal plane, the d orbital has two perpendicular planes, and the s orbital has none

demo_steps.title: s orbital: no node
demo_steps.narration: The s orbital is a single unbroken pink sphere with the nucleus at its center. There is no sign change and no nodal plane anywhere on the surface.

demo_steps.title: p orbital: one node
demo_steps.narration: The p orbital splits into two lobes pinching to zero at the nucleus. The pink lobe and blue lobe have opposite signs, separated by one horizontal nodal plane through the green bead.

demo_steps.title: d orbital: two nodes
demo_steps.narration: The d orbital has four lobes in a cloverleaf with signs alternating pink-blue-pink-blue around the ring, produced by two perpendicular nodal planes crossing at the nucleus.

demo_steps.title: Same-sign lobes
demo_steps.narration: Click a pink lobe: both diagonally-opposite pink lobes highlight together while the blue lobes dim, showing that color encodes wave-function sign, not position.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: nucleus bead = SphereGeometry radius 0.12, green #6aa84f (s bead slightly yellow-green #a8c256). s orbital = SphereGeometry radius 1.0, translucent pink #cf8b93 opacity ~0.85 with soft specular highlight. p orbital = two ellipsoids (radii 0.8,1.0,0.8) centered at y=+1.05 (pink #cf8b93) and y=-1.05 (blue #5b8fd6), tapering toward the origin so they pinch at the nucleus; nodal plane = thin translucent grey disk radius ~1.3 in the XZ plane at y=0. d orbital = four ellipsoids (radii ~0.7,0.7,0.55) centered at distance ~1.15 along the XY diagonals (+1,+1,0),(-1,+1,0),(-1,-1,0),(+1,-1,0) normalized; colors pink at (+1,+1) and (-1,-1), blue at (-1,+1) and (+1,-1); two nodal disks in the XZ and YZ planes. Only the selected orbital is shown, centered at origin; caption text swaps with the toggle. Sign legend small in a corner. Everything fits within radius ~2.2.
interactionPlan.notes: Build each lobe as a scaled SphereGeometry (ellipsoid) with MeshPhongMaterial, transparent true, depthWrite false, and a slight emissive tint so translucency reads like the source. Group lobes by sign ('pos' pink, 'neg' blue) so the click handler can raycast a lobe, read its sign group, and boost emissive/opacity on that group while lowering the other. On toggle, hide the inactive orbital groups and show the active one centered; keep the nucleus bead and nodal-plane disks parented to each orbital group. Recompute raycast targets per visible orbital. Use OrbitControls with damping; default camera at azimuth 35 / elevation 18 to match the slightly three-quarter shaded look of the source renders.

authoredContext:
What do orbitals look like? There are four different kinds of orbitals, denoted s, p, d, and f, each with a different shape. Of the four, we’ll be concerned primarily with s and p orbitals because these are the most common in organic and biological chemistry. An s orbital has a spherical shape, with the nucleus at its center; a p orbital has a dumbbell shape with two parts, or lobes; and four of the five d orbitals have a cloverleaf shape with four lobes, as shown in the figure. The fifth d orbital is shaped like an elongated dumbbell with a doughnut around its middle.

The three different p orbitals within a given shell are oriented in space along mutually perpendicular directions, denoted px, py, and pz. As shown in the figure, the two lobes of each p orbital are separated by a region of zero electron density called a node. Furthermore, the two orbital regions separated by the node have different algebraic signs, + and −, in the wave function, as represented by the different colors in the figure and the figure. As we’ll see in Section 1.11, these algebraic signs for different orbital lobes have important consequences with respect to chemical bonding and chemical reactivity.

Representations of s, p, and d orbitals. An s orbital is spherical, a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, and four of the five d orbitals are cloverleaf-shaped. Different lobes of p orbitals are often drawn for convenience as teardrops, but their actual shape is more like that of a doorknob, as indicated.

A characteristic s, p, and d orbital with the nucleus at the center of each. Two cloverleaf-shaped lobes and four cloverleaf-shaped lobes form the p and d orbitals, respectively.

The orbitals in an atom are organized into different layers around the nucleus called electron shells, which are centered around the nucleus and have successively larger size and energy. Different shells contain different numbers and kinds of orbitals, and each orbital within a shell can be occupied by two electrons. The first shell contains only a single s orbital, denoted 1s, and thus holds only 2 electrons. The second shell contains one 2s orbital and three 2p orbitals and thus holds a total of 8 electrons. The third shell contains a 3s orbital, three 3p orbitals, and five 3d orbitals, for a total capacity of 18 electrons. These orbital groupings and their energy levels are shown in the figure.

discrepancies: Source shows all three orbitals (s, p, d) side-by-side in one image; the generated figure shows only one orbital at a time behind an s/p/d toggle (acceptable multipanel-toggle pattern, but the at-a-glance composition differs)
Generated lobe pink (#cf8b93 at 0.85 opacity) reads as a muted mauve-rose, noticeably darker and less saturated than the source's light salmon-pink
Extra translucent grey nodal-plane discs and a top ψ>0/ψ<0 legend are present in the generated figure but absent from the source
Camera is an angled perspective view (azimuth ~35°, elevation ~18°) rather than the flat front-on framing of the source panels
evaluation.notes: All three orbitals are correctly built (sphere s, vertical pink/blue dumbbell p, diagonal four-lobe cloverleaf d) with nucleus dots, sign coloring, and meaningful toggle + click-to-highlight-sign + demo-step interactions; main weaknesses are the muted pink tone, the angled camera, and extra nodal-plane discs that make the default view diverge from the flat three-across source.
action_items: Brighten and saturate the positive-lobe pink toward the source's light salmon (e.g. raise color value / reduce darkening from opacity+low emissive) so the s and p/d pink lobes match the reference
Make the nodal-plane discs hidden by default (reveal via a toggle or only on orbit) so the initial view matches the clean source rendering
Optionally frame the camera closer to front-on (lower azimuth/elevation) to mirror the source's flat presentation while still allowing orbit
Slightly enlarge the top ψ-sign legend or move it into the side panel so it does not float as tiny text above the orbital

feedback.rationale: All scores are 4–5 with no failure modes, concept and interactivity are excellent, and the remaining issues are minor visual polish (slightly muted pink, extra nodal discs, camera angle) that do not warrant another iteration.
